terse

/TURS/ - rhymes with verse · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Terse means using very few words, sometimes to the point of abruptness.

The lab's terse reply to our forty-line request — 'Resubmit with figures.' — arrived in under a minute.

Example

Grandpa answers the phone the way he ran his hardware store: terse. 'Yep.' 'Nope.' 'Tuesday.' Aunts who need twenty minutes of context call him rude; the regulars knew his shortness held no anger — but strangers on the line can't see his face, and more than one has hung up offended.

Terse is the honest label because it means using very few words, sometimes to the point of abruptness — the shortness itself starts to read as chill. That chill is the line between terse and this unit's succinct: succinct trims fat and stays warm; terse trims fat and lets you feel the knife.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

clipped: Clipped describes the sound of the delivery — words bitten off short, so you can hear the briskness in every syllable. Terse counts the words themselves and lets a little chill ride along. A warm speaker can still sound clipped; terse tells you the frost reached the message.

brisk: Brisk is quick and businesslike with no chill in it at all — the friendly efficiency of a good waiter at the lunch rush. Terse is shortness that has started to cool: nothing rude yet, but you notice the frost. Brisk saves time; terse also withholds warmth.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

chatty: spilling friendly words freely

rambling: wandering on well past the point

Where it sits · how much chill the shortness carries

crisp → terse → gruff

crisp vs. terse: Crisp is milder than terse — efficiency with a smile still possible, quick clean answers that offend no one — while terse lets the shortness carry a little frost.

gruff vs. terse: Gruff goes further than terse — the chill turns to gravel, and the shortness comes out sounding like a growl.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — terse: wiped clean, polished (Latin tersus, from tergere, 'to wipe')

Put it together: Terse is the root: Latin tersus meant 'wiped clean, polished' — a table wiped to the grain, a phrase wiped to the bone. For two centuries English used terse as praise for polished style; the modern chill crept in later, when readers began to feel how cold a perfectly wiped surface can be.

Use the root in a new word: detergent: A detergent is the root still scrubbing: de- + terg-, 'the stuff that wipes grime off.'

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / cool

Terse says the speaker spent the fewest possible words and let the shortness carry a little frost. As praise for tight prose, prefer this unit's succinct; for outright rudeness, you've passed into gruff. Terse sits exactly on the border, and that is its usefulness.
